sample.title: What You're Really Fighting About
paras: Almost every couple has had a fight that started with something tiny: a late reply, a wet towel on the bed, a forgotten errand. Twenty minutes later, both people are hurt and exhausted, and neither can remember how it got so bad.

Sue Johnson, the founder of Emotionally Focused Therapy, describes most couple conflict as a protest against disconnection. When we feel distant from a partner, we get scared, even if we don't recognize it as fear. That fear comes out as anger, criticism, sulking or shutting down. The fight looks like it's about the towel, but underneath, it's a question: Are you still there for me?
Here's an example. Maya texts her partner, Leo, at lunch. He doesn't reply until 9 p.m. When he gets home, she says coldly, "Must've been a busy day." He says, "It was, actually," and it's on.

sample.title: Why Teens Pull Away
paras: One of the hardest parts of parenting teenagers is feeling pushed away. The child who wanted to be with you now prefers friends, keeps their door shut, and seems irritated by your very existence.

It's their job. Psychologists describe adolescence as a period of individuation: becoming a separate individual with your own thoughts, values and life. To do that, teens need to step back from their parents. Sometimes they do it by criticizing you, disagreeing with you, or simply spending more time alone and with friends. It isn't a rejection of you as a person; it's a necessary step toward adulthood.

Friends become central. In adolescence, friends become a primary source of support, identity and belonging. This is normal and important. Teens are learning how to build relationships outside the family, which they'll need for the rest of their lives.

sample.title: Does Worrying Actually Help?
paras: Let's look more closely at those positive beliefs about worrying, because they're often what keeps the habit going. Here are the most common ones, and what's really going on.

"Worrying helps me prepare." Planning helps you prepare. Worry is different. Planning is concrete and leads to action: you make a list, book an appointment, practice a speech. Worry repeats the same fears without moving forward. You can prepare without worrying.

"If I worry, I won't be caught off guard." Think back over your life. Did worrying about something in advance actually make it hurt less when it happened? Most people find it didn't. Instead, they suffered twice: once while worrying, and again when it happened. And most of the things they worried about never happened at all.

sample.title: How Habits Actually Work
paras: A habit is a behavior that has become automatic: you do it in a particular situation without really deciding to. Brushing your teeth before bed. Checking your phone when you wake up. Reaching for a snack when you sit down to watch TV.

Research by the psychologist Wendy Wood and others suggests that a large share of our everyday behavior is habitual, carried out with little conscious thought. That's why willpower alone is such an unreliable way to change. Willpower is needed when you're making a decision. Habits take the decision out of it.
To build a new habit, you need a clear cue, an easy behavior and a satisfying reward. To break an old one, it helps to change or remove the cue.

sample.title: What Inflation Is (and Isn't)
paras: Inflation is a general rise in prices across the economy, which means each dollar buys a little less than it used to.

The key word is general. If coffee gets expensive because of a bad harvest in Brazil, that's a change in one price, driven by supply and demand. Inflation is when prices are rising broadly: food, rent, cars, haircuts, and wages, all drifting up together.

Inflation is usually reported as a yearly percentage. If inflation is 3 percent, something that cost $100 a year ago now costs about $103 on average. That doesn't sound like much, but it adds up. At 3 percent a year, prices roughly double in about 24 years. (Chapter 23 explains a handy trick for working that out.)

sample.title: Where Tarot Came From
paras: Tarot didn't begin as a fortune-telling tool. It began as a card game.

The earliest surviving tarot cards come from northern Italy in the fifteenth century, painted for wealthy families like the Visconti and Sforza of Milan. They were used to play a trick-taking game called tarocchi, a bit like modern bridge, with an extra suit of picture cards, the "triumphs," that beat all the others. People in France, Austria, and other parts of Europe still play tarot card games today.

The link between tarot and mysticism came much later. In 1781, a French writer named Antoine Court de Gébelin claimed, without any real evidence, that the cards preserved secret wisdom from ancient Egypt. The idea caught on. Over the next century, French and British occultists connected the cards to astrology, the Hebrew alphabet, and the four classical elements, and began using them for divination.

sample.title: The Big Three: Sun, Moon and Rising
paras: If you learn only three things about your chart, learn these. Astrologers often call them "the big three," and together they give a surprisingly rounded first portrait.

The Sun: who you're becoming. The Sun represents your core identity, your sense of purpose, what makes you feel alive and proud. It's the self you grow into. Your Sun sign is the one you already know, determined by your birth date.

The Moon: what you need. The Moon represents your emotional nature: how you react, what comforts you, what you need to feel safe, and the habits you fall back on when you're tired or stressed. If the Sun is who you are at your best, the Moon is who you are at home in your pajamas.
